pos: n. (a monk who lives in community under a rule and an abbot, as distinguished from a solitary; the first and, in Benedict's judgement, the strongest kind)
etymology: Late Latin coenobita, from Greek koinos bios, the common life — one who lives the shared life.
biblical_def: Benedict opens his rule by naming four kinds of monk, and he puts the coenobites first and calls them the strongest kind: those who live in a monastery, serving under a rule and an abbot. The other three he names only to dismiss. The judgement is sound, and it is biblical before it is monastic. The Greek behind the word is koinos, common, and the first church in Jerusalem is described with the same root: “neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common” (Act 4:32). The Psalter commends the arrangement with evident warmth: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1). The Preacher gives the practical argument, which is that a man alone has no margin: “woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up” (Ecc 4:10). The common life is not a lower path for those unfit for solitude. In Scripture it is the ordinary shape of Christian obedience.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cenobite as one of a religious order, living in a convent or in community, in opposition to an anchoret or hermit; and community as a society of people having common rights and privileges.
webster_full: CENOBITE, n. One of a religious order, living in a convent or in community, in opposition to an anchoret or hermit, who lives in solitude.
COMMUNITY, n. A society of people, having common rights and privileges, or common interests, civil, political or ecclesiastical.
CONVENT, n. An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns. A house for persons devoted to religion; an abbey; a monastery.
UNITY, n. The state of being one; oneness. Concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company. Retired; remote from society.
scriptures: Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
corruption_summary: The monk of the common life, whom Benedict called the strongest kind, and the Scriptures that agree with him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the long Christian prejudice that solitude is the higher calling and community a concession to weakness. The desert fathers themselves did not teach it, and Benedict explicitly reverses it; but the romance of the hermit has outlived both. Scripture nowhere commends permanent isolation as an ideal, and it repeatedly describes the believer's life as a shared one — “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the common life is not merely useful; the psalm calls it good and pleasant, which is a stronger claim. “for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1) is the whole subject of a short psalm that then compares it to anointing oil and to dew, neither of which is a consolation prize. Modern individualism produces solitaries without deserts, and they are not stronger for it.
roots_summary: Greek koinos bios, the common life; Greek koinos (G2839), common; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Hebrew yachad (H3162), together; Hebrew naim (H5273), pleasant.
roots_lines: Greek koinos bios — the common life, whence coenobite.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; “but they had all things common” (Act 4:32).
Hebrew yachad (H3162) — together, in union; “for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1).
Hebrew naim (H5273) — pleasant, delightful; “how good and how pleasant it is” (Psa 133:1).
Hebrew chaber (H2270) — a companion, an associate; “the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:10).
usage: “of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32) — the first coenobium.
“Behold, how good and how pleasant” (Psa 133:1) — not a concession to weakness.
“for he hath not another to help him up” (Ecc 4:10) — the argument from falling.

pos: n. (in Benedict's rule, the third and worst kind of monk — men living in twos and threes without rule, abbot or testing, their own desires serving as law)
etymology: Late Latin sarabaita, probably from a Coptic word for one who withdraws from the community; used by Cassian and Benedict as a term of censure.
biblical_def: Benedict's third kind of monk is the sarabaite, and he describes them with unusual heat: untested, unformed, soft as lead, living in twos and threes or alone without a shepherd, in their own sheepfolds and not the Lord's, and taking as holy whatever they happen to want. The charge is not that they are lax about food but that they have no external standard: their pleasure is their rule. Scripture has one sentence for this condition and it closes the book of Judges, where it functions as the verdict on an entire era: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Jdg 21:25). Proverbs reduces it to the individual and names him: “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise” (Pro 12:15). The remedy offered is not stricter rules but an ear, and the sarabaite's defining refusal is precisely of correction from outside himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines self-will as obstinacy, stubbornness, the having one's own will; and license as excess of liberty, leave in contempt of law or decorum.
webster_full: SELF-WILL, n. One's own will; obstinacy; stubbornness.
LICENSE, n. Excess of liberty; exorbitant freedom; freedom abused, or used in contempt of law or decorum.
DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement, comprehending instruction in arts, sciences, correct sentiments, morals and manners. Correction; chastisement.
RULE, n. Government; sway; empire; control; supreme command or authority. An established principle or axiom.
OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; fixed firmly in resolution or opinion; not yielding to reason, arguments or other means.
scriptures: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise.
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
corruption_summary: Benedict's worst kind of monk: men whose own pleasure was the rule, with no abbot and no testing.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is self-chosen religion, which looks like devotion and functions as autonomy. The sarabaite keeps whatever observances he finds congenial and drops the rest, and because every item on the list is itself pious the whole arrangement is almost impossible to challenge. The Judges verdict is severe precisely because the people were not irreligious; they had shrines, priests and sacrifices, and no king.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that submission to an authority outside oneself is a condition of growth, not an obstacle to it. “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5) is the root, and correction is the application — “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby” (Heb 12:11). The modern sarabaite assembles a private spirituality from whatever suits, and calls the result authenticity.
roots_summary: Late Latin sarabaita; Hebrew yashar be-enav, right in his own eyes; Hebrew ewil (H191), a fool; Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel; Greek paideia (G3809), chastening or training.
roots_lines: Late Latin sarabaita — Cassian's and Benedict's word for the unruled monk.
Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, right; “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Jdg 21:25).
Hebrew ewil (H191) — a fool, one morally perverse; “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Pro 12:15).
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice; “but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise” (Pro 12:15).
Greek paideia (G3809) — training by discipline; “the peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Heb 12:11).
usage: “there was no king in Israel” (Jdg 21:25) — the condition, stated as a cause.
“but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise” (Pro 12:15) — the remedy is an ear.
“lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5) — the sarabaite's exact refusal.

pos: n. (in Benedict's rule, the fourth and last kind of monk — one who wanders all his life from cell to cell and province to province, a guest everywhere and a member nowhere)
etymology: Late Latin gyrovagus, from Greek gyros, a circle, and Latin vagari, to wander — one who wanders in circles.
biblical_def: Benedict ends his list of monks with the gyrovagues, and declines to discuss them further: always on the move, never settled, three days a guest in one house and then another, slaves of their own appetites, and worse in every respect than the sarabaites. The type depended on Christian hospitality and consumed it. The Didache had already dealt with the problem by the simple rule that an itinerant who stays more than two or three days is a false prophet. The New Testament names the condition precisely and in both sexes. Paul writes of men who “walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies” (2Th 3:11), and of younger widows who “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (1Ti 5:13). The association of restlessness with gossip is not incidental: a man with no settled duties acquires an interest in other people's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vagrant as wandering, unsettled, moving from place to place without any settled habitation; and busybody as a meddling person, one who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others.
webster_full: VAGRANT, a. Wandering; unsettled; moving from place to place without any settled habitation.
BUSYBODY, n. One who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others; a meddling person.
STABILITY, n. Steadiness; stableness; firmness; strength to stand without being moved or overthrown.
IDLE, a. Not employed; unoccupied with business; inactive; doing nothing.
TATTLER, n. One who tattles; an idle talker; one who tells tales.
scriptures: For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies.
And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
Now them that are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.
corruption_summary: Benedict's wandering monk, a guest everywhere and a member nowhere, and the apostolic rule about him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is religious mobility that never submits to anyone. A gyrovague is never under discipline because he is never there long enough to be disciplined, and he is always welcome because nobody has yet had to live with him. The church has produced this type in every century and currently produces it in congregations rather than cells. Paul's remedy is an unsentimental rule about food: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Benedict's great contribution, the vow of stability — the promise to stay in one place with one set of difficult brethren. Paul commands the same thing in substance: “that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread” (2Th 3:12). Quietness, work and one's own bread are the three things a wanderer has arranged his life to avoid.
roots_summary: Latin gyrovagus, a circle-wanderer; Greek ataktos (G814), disorderly; Greek periergos (G4021), a busybody; Greek argos (G692), idle; Greek hesuchia (G2271), quietness.
roots_lines: Latin gyrovagus — from gyros, a circle, and vagari, to wander.
Greek ataktos (G814) — out of rank, disorderly; “walk among you disorderly” (2Th 3:11).
Greek periergazomai (G4020) — to be a busybody; “working not at all, but are busybodies” (2Th 3:11).
Greek argos (G692) — idle, inactive; “they learn to be idle” (1Ti 5:13).
Greek hesuchia (G2271) — quietness, stillness; “that with quietness they work” (2Th 3:12).
usage: “wandering about from house to house” (1Ti 5:13) — the gyrovague, in the first century.
“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the rule that ends the circuit.
“and eat their own bread” (2Th 3:12) — the mark of a settled man.

pos: n. (a solitary who withdraws to the desert or wilderness to pray; the older form of the word hermit)
etymology: Late Latin eremita, from Greek eremites, of the desert, from eremia, a wilderness or lonely place.
biblical_def: The eremite is the desert solitary of the Egyptian and Syrian fourth century — Antony and the thousands who followed him out of the towns — and the word is simply the Greek for a man of the wilderness. The movement cannot be dismissed, because the Gospels record that the Lord himself sought solitude habitually: “in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35), and he commanded a version of it to every disciple: “when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). What Scripture does not do is make the withdrawal permanent. Christ came back from the solitary place to preach in the next towns, and the closet has a door that opens again. The eremitic life takes a rhythm the Gospels show as alternating and freezes one half of it, and the men who did it best, Antony among them, kept being dragged back into the world by people who needed them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eremite as one who lives in a wilderness or in retirement from society, a hermit; and retirement as the act of withdrawing from company or from public notice.
webster_full: EREMITE, n. One who lives in a wilderness, or in retirement from society; a hermit.
RETIREMENT, n. The act of withdrawing from company or from public notice or station. Private abode; habitation remote from public notice.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
CLOSET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy.
CONTEMPLATION, n. The act of the mind in considering with attention; meditation; study; continued attention of the mind to a particular subject.
scriptures: Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Mar 1:38
And he said unto them, Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also: for therefore came I forth.
Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
corruption_summary: The desert solitary, and the Gospel rhythm of withdrawal and return that the eremitic life stops halfway through.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is withdrawal made permanent and then made meritorious. Christ's own solitude is always for something and always ends: he rises before day to pray, and when the disciples find him his answer is “Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also: for therefore came I forth” (Mar 1:38). A solitude that never produces a return has become an end in itself, and the desert fathers' own sayings are full of warnings about exactly that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that withdrawal is commanded and limited in the same breath. “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mar 6:31) is said by Christ to exhausted men, with the reason given that there were so many coming and going that they had no leisure to eat. Rest and the closet are ordinary Christian necessities; neither is a vocation.
roots_summary: Greek eremia, a wilderness; Greek eremos (G2048), desert or solitary; Greek tameion (G5009), an inner chamber; Greek proseuchomai (G4336), to pray; Greek anapauo (G373), to rest.
roots_lines: Greek eremites — of the eremia, the wilderness; whence hermit.
Greek eremos (G2048) — desolate, solitary; “departed into a solitary place” (Mar 1:35).
Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner room, a storeroom; “enter into thy closet” (Mat 6:6).
Greek kruptos (G2927) — secret, hidden; “pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6).
Greek anapauo (G373) — to give rest; “and rest a while” (Mar 6:31).
usage: “a great while before day” (Mar 1:35) — the Lord's own habit.
“when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6) — a door that opens again.
“for therefore came I forth” (Mar 1:38) — the end of every withdrawal.

pos: n. and a. (one shut up in a cell, often walled in beside a church with a window to the altar and another to the street; also, the state of such a life)
etymology: Latin reclusus, shut up, from recludere, to shut away; in medieval usage a technical term for one formally enclosed by a bishop.
biblical_def: A recluse was not merely a shy person. The medieval office of enclosure was liturgical: the bishop read the office of the dead over the candidate, who then entered a cell often built against a church wall, which was sometimes sealed. The cell had a squint into the chancel so that mass could be seen, and a window to the street through which the recluse gave counsel to anyone who came — which is why the most famous English recluse, Julian of Norwich, is known at all. The life has a real and limited warrant in the Lord's own practice of retirement, and a clear boundary set in his prayer for his disciples: “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15). Paul makes the same point as a reductio: avoiding every covetous or immoral person is impossible, “for then must ye needs go out of the world” (1Co 5:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines recluse as shut up, sequestered, retired from the world or from public notice; and seclusion as the act of separating from society or connection, the state of being separate.
webster_full: RECLUSE, a. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.
SECLUSION, n. The act of separating from society or connection; the state of being separate or apart; retirement; privacy; solitude.
ENCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut in; to confine on all sides.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison, or in a monastery or nunnery.
ANCHORET, n. A hermit; a recluse; one who retires from society into a desert or solitary place, to avoid the temptations of the world.
scriptures: I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world.
As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world.
Mat 5:13
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
corruption_summary: The formally enclosed solitary, walled beside a church, and the prayer that asks for keeping rather than removal.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the escape from contamination by subtraction, which cannot work because the contamination travels with the man. The desert fathers knew this and said so repeatedly: a cell cures nothing a heart has brought into it. Christ's prayer does not ask for extraction and the reason is given in the next breath: “As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world” (Joh 17:18) — a sending, not a storing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's distinctness is for the sake of the place he is in. “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Mat 5:13) assumes contact. Salt in the cellar is safe and useless. The recluse's street window, through which Julian counselled anyone who stopped, was the best part of the arrangement and the part most easily sealed.
roots_summary: Latin recludere, to shut away; Greek tereo (G5083), to keep or guard; Greek poneros (G4190), evil; Greek apostello (G649), to send out; Greek halas (G217), salt.
roots_lines: Latin reclusus — shut up, enclosed; the bishop's formal act.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to guard; “that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15).
Greek airo (G142) — to take up, to take away; “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world” (Joh 17:15).
Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth with a commission; “even so have I also sent them into the world” (Joh 17:18).
Greek halas (G217) — salt; “Ye are the salt of the earth” (Mat 5:13).
usage: “but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15) — keeping, not removal.
“for then must ye needs go out of the world” (1Co 5:10) — Paul's reductio.
“wherewith shall it be salted?” (Mat 5:13) — the question a sealed cell cannot answer.

pos: n. (in Eastern monasticism, a small settlement of two or three monks living under an elder, between the solitary cell and the full monastery)
etymology: From Scetis, the Coptic shi-hyt, the desert of Nitria in Egypt where the arrangement began; Greek sketis.
biblical_def: A skete is the Eastern church's middle way. Two or three monks live in a single dwelling or a small cluster under the direction of an elder, keeping their own rule of prayer through the week and coming together with the other sketes for the liturgy. It is neither the full common life of a great monastery nor the solitude of the cell, and it was devised because both extremes had obvious failures: the large house could hide a man, and the cell could unmake him. The arithmetic is the Preacher's. “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9), and the reason given is not productivity but rescue: “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:10). Proverbs supplies the other benefit of a very small company, which is friction: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17). Two or three is also the number our Lord attached to his promised presence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hermitage as the habitation of a hermit, a cell or retired place; and companion as one who keeps company with another, one with whom a person frequently associates.
webster_full: HERMITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a house or hut with its appendages, in a solitary place, where a hermit dwells.
COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates and converses.
ELDER, n. One who is older than another or others. In Scripture, a person who, on account of his age, is appointed or chosen to office.
SHARPEN, v.t. To make sharp; to give a keen edge or fine point to.
DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
corruption_summary: The Eastern settlement of two or three under an elder, a deliberate middle way between the cell and the great house.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near any very small religious company is the closed circle: three men who sharpen one another can also confirm one another in anything, and a group too small to contain disagreement becomes a single mind with three voices. The Eastern practice guarded it by binding every skete to a larger body and a common liturgy. A small group with no accountability outside itself is a sarabaite arrangement with better manners.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the promise attached to the smallest possible gathering is enormous and conditional on one thing only: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20). In my name is the whole condition, and it is what distinguishes a skete from a clique. “Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17) describes a process that is uncomfortable by design.
roots_summary: Coptic shi-hyt, the desert of Scetis; Greek eremos (G2048), wilderness; Hebrew chaber (H2270), a companion; Hebrew barzel (H1270), iron; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather together.
roots_lines: Coptic shi-hyt — the Scetic desert of Nitria, whence the word.
Hebrew chaber (H2270) — a companion; “the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:10).
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, reward; “they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).
Hebrew barzel (H1270) — iron; “Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17).
Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together; “where two or three are gathered together” (Mat 18:20).
usage: “Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the arithmetic of a skete.
“so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17) — friction as a benefit.
“in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the condition that distinguishes a skete from a clique.

pos: n. (in Eastern monasticism, a colony of separate cells grouped along a path around a common church, whose solitaries meet for the Sunday liturgy)
etymology: Greek laura, a lane or alley — from the path between the cells; the arrangement is first recorded in the Judean desert.
biblical_def: A laura, from the Greek word for an alley, is a settlement of hermits who live apart through the week in cells strung along a path or a cliff face, and who come together on Saturday evening and Sunday for the liturgy and a common meal before dispersing again. The great lauras of the Judean desert — Mar Saba above the Kidron, Chariton's at Pharan — held hundreds of men on this pattern for centuries. It is a deliberate attempt to hold two things the church has often set against each other: solitude for the week, assembly for the Lord's day. The second is not optional in Scripture: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching” (Heb 10:25). Nor is the first forbidden. A believer who prays alone six days and gathers on the seventh has the laura's shape without its cliff, and the shape is defensible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assembly as a company or collection of individuals in the same place, usually for the same purpose; and congregation as a collection or assemblage of separate things, an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
webster_full: ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals, in the same place; usually for the same purpose.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assemblage of separate things. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God, and for religious instruction.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison, or in a monastery or nunnery. A small cavity or hollow place.
LANE, n. A narrow way or passage, or a private passage, as distinguished from a public road or highway.
SABBATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employments.
scriptures: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
Act 20:7
And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
A Song of degrees of David. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: A colony of cells along a path, whose solitaries came together for the Lord's day and then went back.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the week without the Sunday — private devotion treated as the whole of religion, with the assembly as an optional supplement for those who like that sort of thing. Hebrews names the habit as already present in the first century: “as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). The laura's discipline is the exact corrective, and it is worth noticing that the solitaries in the Judean desert did not think their solitude excused them from the liturgy; they walked miles to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the stated purpose of gathering, which is mutual provocation to good: “let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works” (Heb 10:24). That is impossible alone and is the thing a week of private prayer cannot supply. The early church fixed the day by practice — “upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread” (Act 20:7) — and the psalmist supplies the proper appetite for it: “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1).
roots_summary: Greek laura, a lane; Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together; Greek paroxusmos (G3948), a provoking or stirring up; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Greek klao arton, to break bread.
roots_lines: Greek laura — a lane or alley; the path between the cells.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).
Greek paroxusmos (G3948) — a stirring up, a provoking; “to provoke unto love and to good works” (Heb 10:24).
Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to exhort; “but exhorting one another” (Heb 10:25).
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house; “Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1).
usage: “as ye see the day approaching” (Heb 10:25) — the reason assembly grows more urgent.
“upon the first day of the week” (Act 20:7) — the day the laura walked to.
“I was glad when they said unto me” (Psa 122:1) — the appetite, not the duty only.

pos: n. (in the Eastern churches, the superior of a monastery or of several monasteries; literally the chief of the fold)
etymology: Greek archi, chief, and mandra, a sheepfold or enclosure — the chief of the fold, an Eastern title answering roughly to abbot.
biblical_def: Archimandrite is the Eastern title for the head of a monastery or a group of them, and its etymology is the whole of its theology: archi-mandrites, the chief of the mandra, the sheepfold. Whoever coined it had read the tenth of John, where the fold, the sheep, the hireling and the shepherd are all defined. The title is therefore a claim and a measurement at once. The measurement is this: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11), which sets the standard for anyone called chief of a fold, and immediately distinguishes him from the hireling who “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13). The claim is more dangerous, because there is only one fold that finally matters and one who gathers it: “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd” (Joh 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines archimandrite as in church history, a chief of a monastery, an abbot; and fold as a pen or inclosure for sheep, and in Scripture the church.
webster_full: ARCHIMANDRITE, n. In church history, a chief of a monastery; an abbot.
FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept. In Scripture, the church, the flock of Christ.
HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages. A mercenary; a prostitute.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals. A Christian church or congregation; the charge of a pastor.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: The Eastern chief of the fold, and the shepherd by whom every such title is measured.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the fold mistaken for the flock — the assumption that the sheep inside one enclosure are the whole of Christ's people. Our Lord explicitly denies it in the same chapter that supplies the word, and the sheep he has elsewhere are brought by his voice and not by the enclosure's gate. Every title that means chief of a fold needs that verse written under it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every under-shepherd is under one, and is answerable at an appearing: “And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away” (1Pe 5:4). Peter writes chief Shepherd deliberately to men he has just called elders, which places the archimandrite, the abbot and the pastor in the same rank and all of them below one person.
roots_summary: Greek archi, chief, and mandra, a fold; Greek poimen (G4166), a shepherd; Greek aule (G833), a fold or courtyard; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Greek archipoimen (G750), chief shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek archi + mandra — the chief of the sheepfold.
Greek poimen (G4166) — a shepherd; “I am the good shepherd” (Joh 10:11).
Greek aule (G833) — a fold, an enclosed court; “which are not of this fold” (Joh 10:16).
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired servant, a hireling; “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).
Greek archipoimen (G750) — the chief Shepherd; “when the chief Shepherd shall appear” (1Pe 5:4).
usage: “giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11) — the measurement of any chief of a fold.
“and they shall hear my voice” (Joh 10:16) — what gathers the flock, not the gate.
“a crown of glory that fadeth not away” (1Pe 5:4) — the only promotion offered.

pos: n. (in the Eastern churches, the head of a monastery; literally the one who leads or goes before)
etymology: Greek hegoumenos, a leader, the present participle of hegeomai, to lead or go before — the same word the New Testament uses of church leaders.
biblical_def: Hegumen is the ordinary Eastern word for the head of a monastery, and unlike abbot it is not borrowed from a family metaphor but taken straight out of the New Testament. Hegoumenos is the participle the writer to the Hebrews uses three times in his closing chapter for the men who lead a congregation, and each use adds a duty. “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) makes the leader's qualification his teaching and the end of his life, not his office. “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) makes obedience owed, and immediately explains why the leader is to be obeyed: he is watching, and he will answer for it. The clause that follows is the sharpest and the most neglected: “that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you” (Heb 13:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preside as to be set over for the exercise of authority, to direct, control and govern; and overseer as one who overlooks, a superintendent.
webster_full: PRESIDE, v.i. To be set over for the exercise of authority; to direct, control and govern, as the chief officer.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor.
RULE, v.t. To govern; to control the will and actions of intelligent beings, by laws, precepts or authority.
SUBMIT, v.i. To surrender; to yield one's person to the power of another; to yield to another in opinion or obedience.
ACCOUNT, n. A computation of debts and credits. A reckoning, or answer to be rendered.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you;
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
corruption_summary: The Eastern word for a monastery's head, taken straight from the New Testament word for a church leader.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is rule understood as rank, which the Lord forbade by name and in the exact vocabulary of this entry: “But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Luk 22:26). The word rendered chief there is the same hegoumenos. A title that means leader is therefore a title the Lord redefined before anyone held it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reciprocity Hebrews builds in. The congregation obeys; the leader watches and will give account; and the congregation is told that making his work grievous is “unprofitable for you” (Heb 13:17) — their own loss, not his. Paul says the same in a gentler register: “know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you” (1Th 5:12).
roots_summary: Greek hegeomai (G2233), to lead or go before; Greek peitho (G3982), to obey or be persuaded; Greek agrupneo (G69), to keep watch; Greek logos (G3056), an account; Greek diakoneo (G1247), to serve.
roots_lines: Greek hegoumenos — one who leads, from hegeomai, to go before.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, to rule; “Remember them which have the rule over you” (Heb 13:7).
Greek agrupneo (G69) — to be sleepless, to watch; “for they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17).
Greek hupeiko (G5226) — to yield, to submit; “and submit yourselves” (Heb 13:17).
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve; “as he that doth serve” (Luk 22:26).
usage: “whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7) — a leader is followed in his faith, not his office.
“as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17) — why obedience is owed.
“let him be as the younger” (Luk 22:26) — the Lord redefining the word itself.

pos: n. (in Russian Orthodoxy, an elder of recognised spiritual discernment to whom others resort for counsel and to whom disciples disclose their thoughts)
etymology: Russian starets, an old man or elder, from the Slavic root for old; answering to the Greek geron, an elder of the desert tradition.
biblical_def: The starets is the Russian form of the desert elder: a monk, often not ordained, sought out for discernment, to whom disciples open their thoughts and from whom they take direction. The institution produced men of genuine stature and was the engine of the nineteenth-century Russian spiritual revival; it also produced, at its worst, the figure of the elder as an unaccountable oracle, which is how Rasputin was able to present himself. Scripture is in favour of counsel and emphatic about its plurality: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — the safety is in the multitude. And it allows exactly one person to stand between God and a man: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Those two verses together both commend the office and fence it: an elder whose counsel can be weighed against other counsel is a gift; an elder whose word cannot be checked has taken a place that is occupied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines elder as one who is older, and in Scripture a person appointed or chosen to office on account of his age and experience; and counsellor as any person who gives advice, one whose profession is to give advice.
webster_full: ELDER, n. One who is older than another, or who has lived to a greater age. In Scripture, a person who, on account of his age, is appointed or chosen to office.
COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; but properly one who is authorized by natural relationship, or by birth, office or profession, to advise another.
DISCERNMENT, n. The act of discerning; also, the power or faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes one thing from another.
MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them. By way of eminence, Christ is the mediator.
DIRECTION, n. Aim at a certain point; a line of motion. Order; prescription, either verbal or written; instruction in what manner to proceed.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: The Russian spiritual elder: a real gift where his counsel can be weighed, and a usurpation where it cannot.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the director who becomes a mediator. The disclosure of thoughts to an elder is a genuinely ancient practice with real value, and it becomes something else entirely the moment the elder's judgement is treated as beyond examination and his blessing as the condition of God's favour. The Russian tradition itself warned against the false elder in exactly these terms, and the warning was needed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of testing, which is laid on the hearer and not on the teacher: “Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jo 4:1). The practical safeguard is plurality, since “in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22). A man with one spiritual director and no other voice has arranged his life so that a single error cannot be caught.
roots_summary: Russian starets, an elder; Greek presbuteros (G4245), an elder; Hebrew tachbulah (H8458), wise counsel or guidance; Greek mesites (G3316), a mediator; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to test or prove.
roots_lines: Russian starets — an old man, an elder; Greek geron in the desert tradition.
Hebrew tachbulah (H8458) — direction, wise guidance; “Where no counsel is, the people fall” (Pro 11:14).
Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise, to counsel; “in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22).
Greek mesites (G3316) — a go-between, a mediator; “one mediator between God and men” (1Ti 2:5).
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; “try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1).
usage: “but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — the safety is in the number.
“and one mediator between God and men” (1Ti 2:5) — the post that is filled.
“believe not every spirit” (1Jo 4:1) — a duty laid on the disciple.
